study.title: Probing the Reionization History and Bubble Sizes with JWST Lyman-$α$ Fraction Measurements

cover.headline: **JWST galaxy data may reveal** when the early universe switched from opaque to clear

slides.title: The fraction of galaxies emitting detectable light at specific wavelengths may tell us when and how reionization happened.
slides.body:
After the Big Bang, neutral hydrogen filled the universe and blocked ultraviolet light. Early galaxies ionized it, creating clear bubbles that merged.

Tracking which galaxies show Lyman-alpha light lets researchers map that transition and estimate bubble sizes.

slides.title: The team reports the universe was 57 percent neutral at redshift 8 and 93 percent neutral at redshift 11.
slides.body:
They compared JWST Lyman-alpha fractions with simulation predictions. The match was good, with reduced chi-squared between 0.4 and 1.2.

At redshift 7, the data suggest roughly 38 percent neutral hydrogen by mass, rising steeply at earlier times.

slides.title: Lyman-alpha photons scatter off neutral hydrogen, so fewer galaxies show the line when more of the medium is neutral.
slides.body:
The researchers used the THESAN simulation and a semi-analytic model. They calibrated intrinsic emission using data from redshift 6.

The fraction of galaxies with detectable Lyman-alpha drops sharply at higher redshifts, tracking the rising neutral fraction.

caveats: This is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed yet, so no independent expert has checked the work.
The bounds are wide and rely on models of both galaxy emission and reionization that carry their own assumptions.

unsupported_claims.claim: The team reports the universe was 57 percent neutral at redshift 8 and 93 percent neutral at redshift 11.
unsupported_claims.problem: The abstract gives ranges with error bars, not single point estimates. At z~8, the abstract reports 0.57^{+0.23}_{-0.57} (or 0.68^{+0.12}_{-0.39}), and at z~11 it reports 0.93^{+0.05}_{-0.17} (or 0.89^{+0.11}_{-0.15}). The copy presents these as definitive 'reports' of 57% and 93% without uncertainty, which misrepresents the findings.

unsupported_claims.claim: At redshift 7, the data suggest roughly 38 percent neutral hydrogen by mass
unsupported_claims.problem: The abstract reports a range of 0.38^{+0.14}_{-0.38} (or 0.52^{+0.09}_{-0.21}) at z~7. The lower bound of the first estimate goes to 0%, making '38 percent' misleadingly precise. The copy should reflect the uncertainty.

source.abstract: Recent James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) measurements quantify the fraction of ultraviolet-selected galaxies showing detectable Lyman-alpha (Ly-$α$) lines at $z \sim 6-14$. These Ly-$α$ fractions are partly shaped by Ly-$α$ scattering from neutral hydrogen in the surrounding intergalactic medium (IGM), and so the observed Ly-$α$ fraction evolution can inform our understanding of the reionization history and the size distribution of ionized bubbles during reionization. We compare the JWST measurements with Ly-$α$ transmission calculations based on both the THESAN reionization simulations and a flexible semi-analytic model. In each case, we calibrate a sub-grid model for the intrinsic Ly-$α$ emission lines emerging from the interstellar medium (ISM) and circumgalactic medium (CGM) of the host galaxies using empirical estimates of the Ly-$α$ equivalent width (EW) distributions at $z \sim 6$. We find that the reionization history and bubble sizes in THESAN yield good agreement with current JWST Ly-$α$ fraction observations, with a reduced $χ^2_ν= 0.4-1.2$. Our semi-analytic models and THESAN Ly-$α$ transmission calculations agree well, allowing us to explore a wide range of reionization models. We derive $1σ$ bounds on the average mass-weighted neutral fractions of: $\langle x_{\mathrm{HI}} \rangle$ = $0.38^{+0.14}_{-0.38}$ ($0.52^{+0.09}_{-0.21}$), $0.57^{+0.23}_{-0.57}$ ($0.68^{+0.12}_{-0.39}$), and $0.93^{+0.05}_{-0.17}$ ($0.89^{+0.11}_{-0.15}$) at $z \sim$ 7, 8, and 11, based on the Ly-$α$ fraction measurements with EW $>25\,\mathring{\rm A}$ ($>10\,\mathring{\rm A}$).
